questions.stem: Skye, a 33-year-old mechanic seen in general practice for 5 months of fatigue, says he gets up 3 or 4 times a night to pass urine. You want to know whether this is true polyuria or frequent small voids from a bladder or prostate problem. Which question best tells them apart?
options: "Does it sting or burn when you pass urine?"
"Are you passing a large amount each time, or only small amounts often?"
"Do you have trouble getting started, or is the stream weak?"
"Do you get a sudden urge to go that is hard to hold on?"
questions.why: Polyuria means a large total volume of urine, so each void is large. Frequency means small amounts passed often. Asking about the volume of each void (or using a voiding diary) separates an osmotic or DI cause from bladder, prostate or infective causes.
notes: This screens for a UTI, but dysuria does not tell you whether the total urine volume is increased.
This screens for outlet obstruction such as prostatic enlargement, which is unlikely at 33, and it does not measure the volume passed.
Urgency suggests an overactive bladder, which causes small frequent voids. It does not show whether he is passing a large volume.

questions.stem: Skye, 33, has new type 2 diabetes in general practice: HbA1c 9.1% (76 mmol/mol), fasting glucose 12.4 mmol/L, urine ketones negative, eGFR over 90, uACR normal, no weight loss. Your GP supervisor will start medication today alongside lifestyle change. Which initial regimen is most appropriate?
options: Gliclazide modified release 30 mg orally each morning as the sole first-line agent
Insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously at night until HbA1c falls below 7%
Metformin 500 mg orally once daily with the evening meal, increased gradually
Metformin 1 g orally twice daily from day one so he reaches target quickly
questions.why: Metformin is first line for type 2 diabetes with normal renal function. Start low with food (e.g. 500 mg daily) and increase every 1 to 2 weeks to limit GI side effects, then recheck HbA1c at 3 months.
notes: A sulfonylurea is a second-line add-on. Used alone first line it causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia and skips metformin, which he can take.
Insulin is for catabolic features, ketosis or failure of oral agents. Skye has no weight loss, negative ketones and has not tried metformin.
Starting at the full dose makes nausea and diarrhoea much more likely and hurts adherence. Titrating slowly is standard.

questions.stem: Skye, 33, has nocturia that persists even when he stops drinking after dinner. His fasting glucose is 12.4 mmol/L and his urine dipstick shows glucose 3+ with specific gravity 1.020. What mechanism best explains why glucose appears in his urine?
options: Insulin deficiency suppresses ADH release, so free water and glucose are lost together
Hyperglycaemia makes the collecting duct resistant to ADH, so glucose leaks into urine
Filtered glucose exceeds the maximum reabsorption of proximal tubule SGLT transporters
Hyperfiltration speeds tubular flow so glucose bypasses reabsorption in the loop of Henle
questions.why: Glucose is normally fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by SGLT2 and SGLT1. Above about 10 mmol/L plasma glucose, the filtered load exceeds this transport maximum. The glucose left in the tubule holds water with it, causing an osmotic diuresis.
notes: Insulin does not regulate ADH release, and ADH deficiency (central DI) produces dilute urine without glucose, unlike Skye's.
Glucose does not cause collecting duct ADH resistance; nephrogenic DI gives dilute, glucose-free urine, whereas Skye's urine is concentrated.
Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, not the loop of Henle, and glycosuria comes from saturating that transport, not from faster flow.

questions.stem: During Skye's focused examination (33, new type 2 diabetes, smoker), you check his peripheral pulses as part of a baseline diabetic foot assessment. Where should you palpate the dorsalis pedis artery?
options: Behind the medial malleolus, midway between it and the calcaneal tendon
Behind the lateral malleolus, alongside the fibularis longus and brevis tendons
In the first web space, between the heads of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals
Lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the proximal dorsum of the foot
questions.why: The dorsalis pedis continues the anterior tibial artery. Feel for it on the proximal dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, over the tarsal bones and bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals.
notes: This is where you feel the posterior tibial artery, the other foot pulse to check in a diabetic foot assessment.
The fibular artery runs deep behind the lateral malleolus and is not normally palpable as a foot pulse.
Distally the dorsalis pedis dives between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals to join the plantar arch, so it is not reliably felt in the web space.
